title: When Your Beliefs Get in the Way of Effective Leadership
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership (Substack)
summary: Kurt Mueller argues that situational leadership effectiveness depends not only on choosing the right leadership orientation but on recognizing how one's beliefs are distorting interpretation of the situation itself. The article offers three diagnostic questions for identifying belief-induced mindset limitations: whether a belief was formed before evidence-based reflection was possible (suggesting it persists by inertia); whether learning it was untrue would cause emotional disturbance (signaling the mind is avoiding disconfirming evidence); and whether one cannot understand how an intelligent person could hold a contrary view (indicating one-sided engagement). Mueller frames the solution not as changing one's position but as changing one's vantage point -- moving to a place where the same situation looks different -- so that arguments become puzzles to understand rather than battles to win. The piece is brief but provides a practical framework for distinguishing between disagreement, situational misreading, and being trapped by unexamined assumptions that limit effective response.
points: * Situational leadership effectiveness has two independent requirements: choosing the right orientation AND recognizing that one's beliefs are influencing what one perceives the situation to be -- failure on either dimension produces misalignment between leadership response and situational need. * First diagnostic: if a belief was formed before deliberate reflection was possible -- from childhood experience, peer habits, emotional reaction, or isolated incident -- it may persist by inertia rather than merit, and every situation deserves a fresh assessment before selecting a response. * Second diagnostic: if discovering a belief was untrue would cause emotional disturbance, the mind is actively veering away from disconfirming evidence -- situationally effective leaders stay curious longer and resist premature conclusions precisely in these moments. * Third diagnostic: inability to understand how an intelligent person could hold a contrary view indicates one-sided engagement with the issue; stakeholders judge success through their own needs, pressures, and priorities, which a leader must genuinely understand to lead effectively. * The mindset shift Mueller prescribes is not position change but perspective shift: adopting the view that others are not wrong but coming from a different place converts arguments from battles to win into puzzles to understand -- a change in vantage point, not a change in conviction.
quotes: Situational effectiveness isn't just about choosing the right leadership orientation. It's also about recognizing that your beliefs are influencing your interpretation of the situation. Some beliefs may not serve you well and contribute to a mindset that sustains a situational misalignment.

Many of our beliefs are acquired long before we even able to reflect on them. They're can be the results of childhood experiences, habits picked up from supervisors or peers, emotional reactions, or traumatic but one-off incidents. Beliefs formed like these, can persist because we haven't yet given it careful (or perhaps any) careful thought.

Our minds tend to veer away from thoughts that disturb us, making it less likely that we believe them, even when they are true. If something is believed to be true and is not, it might create, fear, anxiety and stress by rationally learning the truth. Situationally effective leaders remain curious longer than others. They resist the temptation to rush to conclusions.

When you don't understand how an intelligent person could hold a contrary opinion, that is often an indicator that you have engaged with only one side of an issue, and don't fully understand or weigh the strength of alternative points of view. The challenge is remembering that others, particularly stakeholders may view the same situation very differently.

It asks you to adopt a point of view that other people are not wrong, they are just coming from a different place. Your perspective feels like fact because you've held it long enough, but so does theirs.

The moment you can look at your employee, your colleague, your boss, and genuinely ask 'what are they seeing that I'm not?' everything shifts. The argument stops being a battle to win and starts being a puzzle to understand. You're not changing your position. You're moving your mindset a different place so the view looks different.
